surf.headline: Choose weights that reveal more of the trade-offs.
surf.deck: A weight chooses a compromise. SURF asks how far that choice moves us along the Pareto front—and uses the answer to spread solutions more evenly.
surf.figure_caption: Exact toy scalarization: blue uses equal weight increments; green uses equal arc-length increments. Both objectives are minimized.
steps: Solve weighted problems
Keep a scalarized inner solver and collect its objective vectors.
Reconstruct the distance map
Estimate the cumulative fraction of Pareto-front arc length reached by each weight.
Invert equal quantiles
Choose weights at equal increments of cumulative distance, then solve again.
surf.why: Uniform weights describe the input to the solver. Uniform arc length describes the output geometry. The weight-to-front map generally stretches some intervals and compresses others; its traversal speed supplies the density correction.
reasoning: A scalarization induces a path

Write f_PF(w) for the objective vector at a scalarized optimum. The norm of ∂f_PF(w)/∂w is the speed of that path in objective space. A fixed weight interval can therefore correspond to a very different distance at another part of the front.
Normalize distance into a distribution
Integrating v(w) gives s(w), and normalization gives the paper’s CDF Φ(w). Rule 1 assigns wₙ = Φ⁻¹(n/N), for n = 0, …, N.
Reconstruction creates an error floor

For general problems, SURF reconstructs the map from finitely many solved points and refines it iteratively. Theorem 1 gives geometric contraction toward an O(N⁻²) discretization floor. Increasing N improves that resolution.
notation: Scalarization weight in [0, 1]; the two objective weights are w and 1 − w.
Objective vector at a scalarized optimum, defining the front path in Equation 4.
Speed of that path in objective space.
Cumulative arc length from weight 0 to w. In the integral, p is a dummy weight variable.
Normalized arc length s(w)/s(1), the CDF in Equation 5.
N front segments give N + 1 solution slots indexed by n = 0, …, N.
Current CDF estimate and the reconstructed CDF at outer iteration t.
Damping parameter for the CDF update in Algorithm 1.
surf.result_title: More even coverage, with quality retained
surf.result_context: Reddit summarization with Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and LoRA adapters. These are the KL-regularized objectives in Table 2, evaluated over 10 batches of 64 prompts; values are mean ± standard deviation. Uniform-w and SURF use the same per-slot PPO budget.

chart.title: Spacing coefficient of variation
chart.caption: Lower CV means more even spacing in these reported measurements.

surf.second_result: Hypervolume also rises from 3.76 ± 0.31 for Uniform-w to 4.03 ± 0.35 for SURF. Table 1 separately evaluates MO-Gymnasium tasks; these experiments test both front approximation and coverage.
surf.connection: SURF studies how to allocate solutions across competing objectives. The bilevel papers study a different geometry: how an outer decision interacts with an optimized inner response.

retailagent.headline: Measure whether an agent chooses favorable moments.
retailagent.deck: Holding a stock often and holding it at favorable moments are different behaviors. RetailAgent separates exposure from timing to audit sequential LLM decisions.
retailagent.figure_caption: Reported timing alpha: −45.7 bps, with 95% interval [−49.4, −41.8]. Qwen3.5 text condition; Table 1.
steps: Control the information
Show anonymized intraday history, then require a long-or-flat decision before the next return.
Remove mean exposure
Compare each schedule with constant exposure on the same realized stock-day.
Disrupt the sequence
Shuffle saved actions and examine matched memory panels to characterize sequential structure.
retailagent.why_title: The comparison stays on the same price path
retailagent.why: A stock’s overall movement affects both an agent and a constant-exposure comparator. Subtracting that comparator focuses the score on when the agent allocated its exposure. Negative timing means relatively unfavorable allocation on the evaluated path.
reasoning: Center the action sequence

For a stock-day, p̄_id is the fraction of intervals spent long. The constant-exposure comparator earns p̄_id times the sum of interval returns. Subtracting it from the schedule’s return gives the timing sum shown below.
Separate direction from sequential alignment

A policy that is always long or always flat has zero centered timing. A nonzero score requires variation in its actions and alignment with subsequent returns. This explains why action persistence and switching behavior matter to the audit.
Shuffling and sampling frames

Same-day shuffling preserves each day’s action count while breaking interval alignment. Global shuffling draws from the saved archive. Each modality and memory panel specifies its stock-day frame, conditioning, and sample count.
notation: Stock and trading-date indices. Together they identify one stock-day.
Decision-interval index and total number of intervals in that stock-day.
Binary action before interval t: long (1) or flat (0).
Following interval’s research-return label, revealed after the action.
Mean long exposure over the stock-day.
Exposure-matched timing score in Equation 1. The tables average stock-day scores.
Memory window: number of earlier memories supplied in addition to the current memory.
retailagent.result_context: Table 1, principal 10-minute Qwen3.5 text condition. The intact condition contains 13,710 stock-days. The reported 95% interval for intact timing is [−49.4, −41.8] bps. The chart compares the magnitudes of negative timing, with the signed values printed explicitly.
retailagent.result_reference: Table 1 · Text timing and shuffle controls

chart.title: Timing alpha (bps)
chart.caption: All three reported values are negative; bar length represents magnitude.

retailagent.second_result: The matched memory analyses examine action persistence and timing conditional on switching, linking the timing pattern to the evaluated agents’ sequential behavior.
retailagent.connection: RetailAgent focuses on the timing of sequential choices. SURF offers another view of decision quality: how well a set of choices represents different objective trade-offs.

birq.headline: Let a speech model improve its own training targets.
birq.deck: BiRQ turns intermediate speech representations into pseudo-labels, while raw-input targets anchor the learner as those representations evolve.
birq.figure_caption: Measured word error rates in Table 2: 155M Conformer, 960h pretraining and 100h labeled fine-tuning. Lower is better.
steps: Reuse internal features
Take intermediate representations from the speech model and randomly quantize them.
Keep an input-based anchor
Retain pseudo-labels derived from raw audio features alongside the enhanced targets.
Train the interaction
Use the bilevel formulation and differentiable Gumbel-softmax selection for end-to-end learning.
birq.why_title: Richer targets introduce a feedback loop
birq.why: Intermediate features can carry more useful information than raw-input quantization, but they change during training. The raw-input branch supplies an anchor while the model participates in constructing its enhanced targets.
reasoning: The target generator shares the learner’s representations
BiRQ applies random-projection quantization to intermediate features from the encoder being trained. Those features supply the enhanced target labels.
An anchor and an enhanced target have distinct roles
Raw-input labels provide a fixed reference task. Enhanced labels draw on the evolving learned features. Both sources contribute to the masked-frame prediction objective.
Selection connects the discrete and trainable components

The method uses differentiable Gumbel-softmax selection within its bilevel training framework. Section 3 gives the losses and update scheme. Algorithm 1 specifies how gradients from both label sources enter training.
notation: Unmasked normalized speech sequence and its masked view.
Parameters of the shared acoustic encoder.
Target-generating intermediate layer and total encoder depth.
Enhanced-label and anchor-label masked-frame cross-entropy losses.
Anchor-loss feasible set and its allowed gap above the optimum. θ′ is the variable in the anchor-loss minimum.
Enhanced and anchoring loss weights. Their ratio is the penalty constant in Equation 9.

birq.result_context: Table 2, C2 setting: 10-layer 155M Conformer, 960h LibriSpeech self-supervised pretraining, then 100h labeled fine-tuning. The comparison below is test-other WER; test-clean is 6.8% for BEST-RQ and 5.0% for BiRQ.

birq.second_result: Table 3 tests a different setting: a 275M Conformer pretrained on 5k hours of YODAS and fine-tuned on 150h of AMI. WER is 18.4% versus 16.3% on ami-ihm and 37.2% versus 34.0% on ami-sdm for BEST-RQ and BiRQ.
birq.connection: BiRQ uses bilevel structure to connect a learner with its target construction. PBGD-Free investigates a separate algorithmic question: when flatness can reduce the cost of a nested optimization problem.

efficient-penalty.headline: Reduce the work inside a bilevel training step.
efficient-penalty.deck: Reduced-curvature analysis permits larger outer steps. Flatness-based updates remove one response computation, with separate methods for fixed and coupled constraints.
efficient-penalty.figure_title: Two constraint regimes, two loop structures
efficient-penalty.figure_caption: PBGD-Free is fully single-loop in the analyzed uncoupled case. With general coupled constraints, the proposed method retains an inner solve. Sections 4–5.
steps: Analyze the reduced objective
Analyze curvature along the optimized lower-level response to obtain a penalty-independent smoothness order.
Use upper-level flatness
Control the effect of dropping the value-function correction when the stated flatness condition holds.
Account for constraints
Distinguish fixed lower-level domains from feasible sets that move with the outer variable.
efficient-penalty.why_title: Efficiency has more than one bottleneck
efficient-penalty.why: Outer step size, value-function response tracking, and coupled-constraint solves contribute separately to the computation. The paper gives a smoothness analysis and update rules for each constraint regime.
reasoning: Cancellation changes the smoothness analysis

Fγ = γ(vγ − v) is built from nearby value functions. Their directional curvature terms can cancel. Theorem 3.1 establishes O(1) reduced smoothness with fixed constraints; Theorem 5.1 extends it under Assumptions 1–5 for coupled constraints.
Flatness changes which correction is necessary
Upper-level flatness controls the objective’s sensitivity to lower-level deviations. That structure bounds the bias from omitting the value-function contribution in PBGD-Free.
Coupled constraints change the remaining work
When c(x, y) depends on x, multipliers enter the value-function derivative. The coupled PBGD-Free method retains an inner loop to estimate the constrained response.
notation: Penalty constant on the lower-level optimality gap.
Base lower-level domain, fixed feasible set, and feasible set depending on x.
Original and perturbed lower-level minimum values, defined below. y_g and y_γ are the respective minimization variables.
Reduced penalty objective after minimizing over the feasible lower variable.
Constraint multiplier at an original lower-level optimum.
Exponent and residual in the upper-level flatness condition used for PBGD-Free.
efficient-penalty.result_title: Match the update to the constraint regime
efficient-penalty.result_context: Read each result with its algorithm, constraint regime, stationarity metric, and inner-solve work.
efficient-penalty.second_result: The SVM benchmark compares accuracy and training time under a recorded stopping rule; the coupled PBGD-Free method retains an inner solve.
efficient-penalty.connection: This preprint extends the value-function removal developed in the NeurIPS 2025 PBGD-Free paper. The EUSIPCO 2025 paper establishes the sharper reduced-smoothness analysis.

pbgd-free.headline: Use one update per level instead of repeated inner solves.
pbgd-free.deck: PBGD-Free uses upper-level flatness to bound the bias from removing the value-function loop, yielding a single-loop penalty method.
pbgd-free.figure_caption: Definition 1 bounds upper-objective variation around a lower-level optimum using exponent α and residual δ.
steps: Identify a flat upper objective
Bound how the upper loss changes when y moves away from a lower-level solution.
Drop the value-function loop
Use the upper partial gradient in the simplified PBGD-Free update.
Control the remaining bias
Analyze convergence with the flatness parameters and the paper’s other assumptions.
pbgd-free.why_title: Flatness controls the bias from omission
pbgd-free.why: Removing the value-function correction saves a response computation. The omitted term creates a bias, which the analysis bounds using upper-level flatness.
reasoning: The penalty magnifies response error

The difference between original and perturbed lower-level responses enters the penalty gradient with a factor γ. Controlling the resulting bias requires the upper-loss sensitivity captured by flatness.
Flatness measures upper-loss sensitivity

Definition 1 states |f(x, y_g^*(x)) − f(x, y)| ≤ c‖y_g^*(x) − y‖^α + δ. The residual δ permits local variation, while α controls how the distance contribution shrinks near a lower-level optimum. The paper generally studies δ > 0 and α > 1.
Flatness enters the convergence bound
The single-loop method tracks the perturbed lower response and updates x using ∇xf. Theorem 3 combines flatness with lower-level regularity to quantify the stationarity error and its residual.
notation: Joint and reduced penalty objectives in Equation 2. z is the lower-variable dummy in the inner minimum.
Set of lower-level minimizers of g and a solution in that set.
Set of minimizers of the joint penalty objective and a solution in that set.
Flatness modulus, distance exponent, and residual in Definition 1.
Outer-iteration index and budget, followed by lower-tracking-step index and budget.

Outer and lower tracking step sizes in Algorithm 1.

pbgd-free.result_context: Table 2 compares parameter-efficient fine-tuning of Llama-3-3b with a fixed training-time budget. Its first column evaluates DPO loss at the trained outcome. The post-SFT outcomes are separate columns.

pbgd-free.connection: The efficient-penalty preprint extends the smoothness analysis and flatness-based updates to fixed and coupled constraints.

The outer direction is the upper partial gradient; the original value-function correction is omitted under the analyzed flatness conditions.

smoothness.headline: Keep outer steps stable as the penalty grows.
smoothness.deck: Penalty methods can look increasingly stiff as the penalty grows. Follow the optimized lower-level response, and the reduced objective can have a different curvature scale.
smoothness.figure_title: Analyze the objective the outer loop follows
smoothness.figure_caption: The joint penalty bound scales with γ. Analyzing the reduced formulation yields O(1) smoothness through directional-curvature cancellation in Sections III–IV.
steps: Separate joint from reduced
Distinguish changing (x, y) freely from moving x while tracking an optimized lower-level response.
Compare nearby value functions
Use second-order directional derivatives to retain cancellation in γ(vγ − v).
Revise iteration accounting
Translate the sharper reduced bound into the paper’s outer-iteration result and count inner solves separately.
smoothness.why_title: Bounding each term separately can lose the mechanism
smoothness.why: The reduced objective is a scaled difference of two closely related value functions. Treating their curvatures as unrelated can keep the factor γ. The directional-derivative analysis retains their relationship and exposes cancellation.
reasoning: A joint bound answers a different question
The penalty acts strongly on departures from lower-level optimality. Joint smoothness sees those directions even when the outer method is intended to follow the lower-level response.
A difference of nearby functions needs a joint analysis
Fγ(x) = γ[vγ(x) − v(x)]. The paper analyzes second-order directional derivatives of that difference, using proximity of the perturbed and original lower-level solutions and the stated regularity.
The rate uses a specific stationarity criterion
The outer iteration order improves from O(ε⁻¹·⁵) to O(ε⁻¹) for the squared generalized-gradient criterion. Total complexity also includes the response-solve work for the chosen constraint regime.
notation: Penalty constant in the joint objective.
Upper domain, base lower domain, and lower feasible set depending on x.
Original and perturbed lower-level minimum values. y_g and y_γ are the corresponding minimization variables.
Joint penalty objective and its reduced objective after lower minimization.
Original and perturbed optimal lower responses.
Original lower-level constraint multiplier in Equation 7.
Unit direction and second-order directional derivative along d.
Outer step size and projected-gradient mapping, defined below.
Tolerance for the squared generalized-gradient norm. Proj denotes Euclidean projection onto the indicated domain.
smoothness.anchor: Sections III–IV · Reduced smoothness and convergence
smoothness.result_context: The paper revisits ALT-PBGD and BLOCC under uncoupled and coupled constraints. The comparison uses the squared generalized-gradient stationarity criterion for the penalty formulation. Inner-solve costs introduce additional factors.
smoothness.second_result: The improvement follows from cancellation between nearby value functions in the reduced formulation, allowing a penalty-independent outer step-size order.
smoothness.connection: BLOCC supplies the earlier primal-dual penalty approach for coupled constraints. The efficient-penalty preprint places the smoothness analysis alongside new updates and flatness in a broader framework.

blocc.headline: Changing constraints changes the best response.
blocc.deck: In a coupled bilevel problem, the outer decision changes the inner feasible set. BLOCC uses primal-dual information to keep that moving boundary in the optimization.
blocc.figure_title: A moving boundary / exact toy problem
blocc.figure_caption: In Figure 1, the constraint g^c(x, y) = 3x − y gives y_g^*(x) = 3x. The multiplier-weighted boundary term restores the value gradient.
steps: Model the changing feasible set
Represent the follower’s moving feasible set using g^c(x, y) ≤ 0.
Track primal and dual information
Use lower-level solutions and constraint multipliers in the penalty reformulation.
Update with first-order information
Analyze approximation and convergence under the stated convexity and regularity assumptions.
blocc.why_title: At an active constraint, the boundary is part of the response
blocc.why: If the follower’s optimum lies on a moving boundary, changing x affects the feasible choices as well as the objective. The constraint multiplier captures the contribution that an objective-only description would miss.
reasoning: The lower-level value changes through two routes
The derivative of v(x) contains an objective term ∇xg and a constraint term involving μ_g^*(x) and ∇xg^c. The multiplier-weighted term accounts for the movement of active constraints.
The toy example makes the multiplier tangible
In Figure 1, y_g^*(x) = 3x and μ_g^*(x) = 2x for x > 0. The partial objective derivative is −4x, while the constraint term contributes 6x. Together they give the true value gradient 2x.
Primal-dual responses support the penalty update

BLOCC uses primal-dual responses in its first-order penalty updates. Strong convexity in y, convex lower-level constraints, domain feasibility, smoothness, and LICQ support the approximation and convergence analysis.

chart.title: Test accuracy / diabetes

blocc.second_result: Section 4.3 studies infrastructure planning on synthetic networks and a 26-node network based on Seville. These applications put the same modeling point into practice: the outer design affects the lower-level choices.
blocc.connection: The EUSIPCO 2025 paper sharpens the smoothness analysis of this penalty framework. The efficient-penalty preprint develops the broader analysis and the flatness-based update extension.
